newsitem.title: UK: S&P ups CNA Intl Reinsurance claims paying rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P ups CNA Intl Reinsurance claims paying rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Friday it had raised its claims-paying ability rating of CNA International Reinsurance Co Ltd (CNAI) to A plus from BBB plus.

"The rating action reflects S&P's view that CNAI is a strategically important subsidiary of its U.S. parent. The upgrade is also partly driven by S&P's belief that CNAI is exhibiting improved rating characteristics in its own right," S&P said in a statement.
It said CNAI is a medium-sized international reinsurer, and is owned by Continental Casualty Co, the largest member of the CNA Intercompany Pool (claims-paying ability A plus).
-- CNAI would continue to diversify geographically, with near-term growth being most marked in European markets. Thus, the dependence on the U.S. market was expected to decline further.
-- The combined ratio would weaken from the 1995 level. Bottom-line results will continue to benefit from the greater contribution made by investment income.
-- S&P expected risk-based capital adequacy to improve and stabilise at a level more consistent with the rating grade.
S&P said major rating factors included the following.
-- CNAI will be an important part of the CNA Group and had a key role to play as the group sought to fulfill one of its primary strategic objectives -- to expand into markets outside the U.S.
-- CNAI had a recognised leading position in its chosen specialised insurance and reinsurance fields. This afforded it significant influence over premium rates and policy terms and conditions.

-- After several years of mediocre results, 1995 produced a combined ratio of 95.2 percent, compared to the previous three years which averaged 108.5 percent. Although 1995 was an exceptional year, S&P believed that CNAI had significantly improved its methods of monitoring and controlling aggregate exposures, to the extent that the combined ratio was unlikely to return to the level seen in 1992 (117.9 percent).

-- CNAI enjoyed a significant advantage due to the stop-loss protection it had in respect of 1990 and prior underwriting years. As a result, any deterioration of asbestos and pollution reserves would not affect CNAI's capital position.

-- The London subscription market was expected to remain CNAI's primary business source, but it was anticipated that growth through an expanding network of European branches would continue to reduce this dependence.

-- In recent years, the U.S. medical malpractice sector had become extremely competitive, following a period of strong profitability. At the same time, many of the U.S. doctors' mutuals were either merging or had grown to a size where they were now able to retain more risk for own account.
S&P said these considerations led it to believe that CNAI's current position in this market would, in the long-term, be difficult to maintain.
-- S&P regarded CNAI's stand-alone risk-based capitalization as modest, but nevertheless adequate.
